list.listitem: Suspect acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in patients with symptoms and signs related to cytopenias. C
Initial diagnostic testing should include CBC, chemistries, coagulation studies, and bone marrow with cytochemistry and immunophenotyping. C
Current management strategies for adult patients with ALL require a careful assessment of relapse risk at treatment initiation. B
Chemotherapeutic regimens based on the Berlin-Frankfurt-Muenster (BFM) regimens are recommended for children and young adults. Hyper-CVAD is a good alternative for adult patients. C
Monoclonal antibodies such as blinatumomab and inotuzomab are promising treatments especially for relapsed disease. B
Monitoring minimal residual disease (MRD) is important to establish therapeutic approach and aids important decisions such as stem cell transplantation (SCT) in high-risk patients. C

About 80% of patients achieve a complete remission (CR) after the first cycle, but 30% to 40% are cured. Induction and maintenance treatment are important to eradicate MRD, as well as CNS prophylaxis. A

background.definition: ALL is a heterogeneous group of lymphoid disorders resulting from a monoclonal proliferation and expansion of immature lymphoid cells in the bone marrow, blood, and other organs. The initial leukemogenic event may occur in lymphoid cells (B or T lineage) or in early hematopoietic precursors. The various ALL subtypes subsequently arise according to the stage of lymphoid differentiation at the time of the leukemogenic event.

list.listitem: The overall incidence of ALL is 1 to 1.5 per 100,000 persons per year.
ALL represents about 80% of childhood acute leukemias (4-5 per 100,000 persons per year), with a peak at 4 to 5 years.
ALL is 20% of adult leukemias (2 per 100,000 persons per year) with a second smaller pick in the elderly. Median age is between 25 and 35 years.

In most cases, the cause of ALL remains unknown. In the favored theory, leukemogenesis reflects the interaction between host susceptibility and environmental factors. A possible genetic predisposition has been recognized (association observed with trisomy 21, and Klinefelter's disease).
There is a high risk of ALL in some inherited diseases (Fanconi's anemia, Bloom's syndrome, ataxia telangectasia).
Association with viral infections (human T-cell lymphotropic virus 1, Epstein-Barr virus [EBV], HIV) has been observed.

Environmental factors such as exposure to radiation, chemical toxins, and cigarette smoking are controversial. A pooled analysis found only a weak association between increasing exposure magnetic fields and childhood leukemia.
Polymorphism of folate-related genes is associated with a decreased risk of ALL in adults.

In pediatric leukemias, recent studies have indicated that the majority of chromosome translocations and preleukemic clones arise in the uterus during fetal hematopoiesis, with secondary genetic events occurring postnatally.
Suspect ALL in patients with symptoms and signs related to cytopenias, such as bleeding, recurrent infections, and anemia. C
Initial diagnostic testing should include CBC, chemistries, coagulation studies, and bone marrow with cytochemistry and immunophenotyping. C
Examination of bone marrow aspirate is preferable for diagnosis of ALL because 10% of patients lack circulating blasts and because bone marrow cells are better than blood cells for genetic studies. C

Define ALL subtypes (which respond differently to therapy and have different prognosis) by assessing morphology, flow cytometry immunophenotyping, cytogenetic/molecular analysis, and genomic profiling. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Recent viral infection, normal Hb, no leukocyte abnormalities
Terminal deoxynucleotide transferase (TdT) negativity, no clonality
Serology RNA/DNA-polymerase chain reaction (PCR) positive for EBV, cytomegalovirus, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, HIV, etc.
Pancytopenia in advanced stages, CD19/CD5 coexpression
Cytochemistry positive for myeloperoxidase (MPO; only 3%-5% of ALL express MPO)
Positive autoimmunity screening (FAN, extractable nuclear antigen, anti-DNA), rheumatoid factor, ESR

list.listitem: There are two recognized classifications:

The French American British Cooperative Group distinguishes 3 ALL groups (L1-L3) based on morphologic criteria (cell size, cytoplasm, nucleoli, basophilia, vacuolation): L1 morphology (small, heterogeneous lymphocytes) has the best rate of CR and 3-year survival of 40% to 75%; it's the most frequent in childhood; L2 morphology (large, heterogeneous lymphocytes) is the most frequent in adulthood; L3 morphology (large, vacuolated, basophilic lymphocytes) is associated with mature B-cell ALL (Burkitt's leukemia) and is characterized by a high rate of cell turnover giving rise to the "starry sky" pattern on marrow biopsies.
The World Health Organization (WHO) proposed new guidelines for the diagnosis of neoplastic diseases of hematopoietic and lymphoid tissues or lymphomas (see ).
Symptom onset is rapid and generally reflect bone marrow failure or leukemic infiltration of extramedullary sites.
Up to 50% of patients have fever or documented infections (neutropenia), and one-third have bleeding at diagnosis (ecchimosis, petechiae); severe hemorrhage is uncommon (thrombocytopenia).

Fatigue, lethargy, dizziness, dyspnea, and cardiac angina may reflect the severity of anemia. Bone pain and arthralgias occur in one-fourth of patients and are more common in children. One-half of adult patients have hepatomegaly, splenomegaly (entity more pronounced in children), or lymphoadenopathy. Mediastinal masses (thymus) occur primarily with T-lineage ALL. A bulky mass can lead to the superior vena cava syndrome or superior mediastinal syndrome.
CNS symptoms occur in fewer than 10% (mostly in B mature ALL with CNS involvement).
Leukemic cells can also be found in other extramedullary sites, including the testis, retina, and skin.

When ALL is suspected, initial diagnostic testing should include history and physical examination, CBC, chemistries, and coagulation studies. In case of pancytopenia with leukopenia or leukocytosis, consider cytomorphology on peripheral blood smears. Bone marrow aspiration or biopsy is mandatory for diagnosis of ALL. Immunophenotyping and cytogenetic analysis are complementary to morphology and cytochemistry in order to address a therapeutic choice.

CBC: Leukopenia is seen in most patients, with hyperleukocytosis (>100,000 WBCs/mm3) in 10% to 16% of patients. Leukemia blasts can be detected in peripheral blood. Other findings are anemia and low platelets (<50,000) in 50% of patients.

Chemistries: Because of a large leukemic cell burden, a tumor lysis syndrome can develop; therefore investigate all patients for kidney function and uric acid at baseline and followed up during treatment. Also investigate renal and liver function before starting any treatment, due to the toxicity that chemotherapy can cause. (10%-20% of patients present with mild liver function alteration as a result of liver infiltration.)

Cytomorphology on bone marrow smears: obtain bone marrow by aspiration and biopsy. The WHO classification defines acute leukemia as more than 20% blasts in marrow and/or blood. In case this is confirmed, order cytochemistry on bone marrow samples.
Cytochemistry: Check for myeloperoxidase (MPO) and TdT to differentiate myeloid from lymphoid phenotype.
Flow cytometry: used for classification in B-cell and T-cell ALL. Typical B-lineage ALL markers include CD10, CD19, CD22, CD79a, and CD20; T-lineage markers include: CD2, CD3, CD5, CD7, and CD8.
Cytogenetic analysis: Karyotype is one of the most important predictors of disease-free survival. Normal karyotype is associated with a 50% 3-year survival (see ).
Molecular analysis: PCR can identify molecular abnormalities derived from detected or undetected chromosomal abnormalities. Many of them can be targets for new drugs (see ).

Analysis of methylation status leads to identification of a hypermethylator phenotype (simultaneous methylation of two or more specific genes) associated with a worse outcome. On this basis, hypomethylating agents may be used.
CXR: A baseline CXR should be performed because of infections due to disease-related immunosuppression. Infections can occur as a complication of the aplasia following chemotherapy.
CT scan/MRI of the brain: For patients with major neurologic signs or symptoms at diagnosis, appropriate imaging studies should be performed to detect meningeal disease or CNS bleeding.

Lumbar puncture should be performed if no mass/lesion is detected on imaging studies and in any case of ALL diagnosis, even if neurologic signs or symptoms are absent. The diagnosis of CNS leukemia requires the presence of more than 5 WBC/μL in the CSF and identification of lymphoblasts in the CSF differential.
See algorithm in .

Goals of treatment are: rapid achievement of a CR (CR: achievement of neutrophil and platelet count recovery with less than 5% marrow blasts); elimination of minimal residual disease (MRD); and treatment of sanctuary sites (see ). Guide treatment by immunophenotype and cytogenetic/molecular tests. A

Mature B-cell ALL: Short and intensive chemotherapy regimens with high-dose methotrexate and cyclophosphamide, as well as intensive CNS prophylaxis (high rates of relapses) are indicated. No maintenance therapy is required. The combination of hyper-CVAD and rituximab improves CR (89%) and survival rates (3-year survival: 80%), especially for patients older than 60 years. A

Ph-positive ALL: Translocation t(9;22) (Philadelphia [Ph] chromosome) has the worst prognosis in all age groups. Imatinib followed by immediate postremission SCT and combined with chemotherapy is associated with improved clinical results. TKI maintenance following transplant is now standard of care in Ph+ group patients. Other tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) with activity against imatinib-resistants include nilotinib and dasatinib. A
Treat ALL in young adults and adolescents with recommended pediatric regimens in multidisciplinary teams (NICE). C

Resistant or relapsed disease: The only potentially curative approach is to achieve a second CR, followed by allogenic SCT. However, with current salvage chemotherapy drugs, the CR rate is low (<50%) and of very short duration, which inhibits many patients from the opportunity to undergo SCT. B
Monoclonal antibodies such as blinatumomab and inotuzomab are promising treatments especially for relapsed disease. B

The management of ALL in adults is based on the model used in treating pediatric patients, which is designed to induce remission, followed by 1 or more cycles of intensification, prolonged maintenance lasting 2 to 3 years, and CNS prophylaxis.

Induction: usually based on the backbone of the pediatric BFM regimen, including a combination of vincristine, corticosteroids, and anthracyclines. This combination achieves CR rates of 75% to 92%, with a median remission duration of around 18 months and a disease-free survival of 29% to 40% Such survival is highest (60%-70%) in T-cell ALL and currently in Burkitt ALL. Clinical trials are investigating the role of L-asparaginase. Dexamethasone is often substituted for prednisone because of better in vitro antileukemic activity and achievement of higher drug levels in the CSF. Hyper-CVAD is a dose-intensive regimen of hyperfractionated cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, and dexamethasone, alternating with high doses of cytarabine and methotrexate for a total of 8 induction and intensified consolidation courses with a CR of 92% and a 5-year survival rate of 38%.
Consolidation: The value of intensification treatment is not certain in adult ALL.

CNS prophylaxis: Without CNS prophylaxis, 50% of patients experience CNS relapses. Recent studies suggest that effective CNS prophylaxis can be achieved without cranial irradiation. The number of intrathecal injections depends on the risk of CNS relapse. Presenting features associated with an increased risk of CNS relapse in adults include mature B-cell ALL, serum lactate dehydrogenase levels, and a high proportion of bone marrow cells in a proliferative state (>14% of cells in S+G2M phase of the cell cycle).
Maintenance: omitting this phase results in higher relapse rate.

Bone marrow transplantation: The use of autologous transplantation in patients not eligible for allogenic SCT is inferior to consolidation/maintenance chemotherapy. Allogenic bone marrow transplantation was superior for standard-risk, but not high-risk patients because of the increased transplantation-related mortality in this group.

Resistant or relapsed disease: the only potentially curative approach is to achieve a second CR, followed by allogenic hematopoietic (H)SCT. New drugs have been developed to reinduce a CR. Nelarabine is a new nucleoside analog approved by the FDA for third-line treatment of adults and children with relapsed/refractory T-cell ALL or T-lymphoblastic lymphoma. Clofarabine induces a 20% CR in relapsed ALL patients. The drug is approved as third-line treatment of pediatric patients with relapsed or refractory ALL.

Imatinib and second-generation TKIs (dasatinib and nilotinib) have drastically improved the prognosis of Ph-positive ALL; rituximab is a monoclonal antibody that targets CD20 antigen, expressed with an adverse prognostic significance on precursors and mature B-cells. Adding rituximab to standard ALL regimen improves 2 year event free survival. Hypomethylating agents like decitabine may be used on this basis of the methylation status.

Antibody therapies in development show some promise, including blinatumomab for relapsed/refractory disease and anti-CD22 (inotuzumab ozogamicin), which has shown response and survival benefit in relapsed disease. In a an RCT with 405 patients randomized to blinatumomab or chemotherapy, the median overall survival was 3.7 months longer in the blinatumomab group.

A study randomized 1440 children with newly diagnosed standard-risk B-cell ALL with an average or higher risk of relapse to chemotherapy alone or chemotherapy plus two 28 day cycles of blinatumomab. The study was terminated early because after 2.5 years disease-free survival was 96% with blinatumomab compared with 88% without (p < 0.001; NNT = 12).

A study randomized 224 patients with MRD negative remission of B-cell precursor ALL to 4 cycles of blinatumomab + consolidation chemotherapy or consolidation chemotherapy alone. After 3 years, overall survival was better in the blinatumomab group (85% vs 68%, p = 0.002, NNT = 6).

In a single arm study of 63 patients with Ph positive ALL, dasitinib plus glucocorticoid for induction was followed by 2 cycles of blinatumomab. Complete remission was seen in 98%, and the overall survival was 95% at 18 months with disease free survival in 88%.

A study randomized 108 children with high-risk first-relapse B-ALL in morphologic complete remission (<5% blasts) or who had M2 marrow (between 5% and 25% blasts) to blinatumomab or a third round of consolidation chemotherapy. After 22 months, numerically fewer deaths occurred in the blinatumomab group (14.8% vs 29.6%, HR 0.43, 95% CI 0.18-1.01) and event-free survival was improved (31% vs 57%, p <0.001, NNT = 4). There were also fewer adverse events in the blinatumomab group.

A study randomized 208 patients age 1 to 30 years with initial B-ALL relapse to blinitumomab or 2 cycles of multiagent chemotherapy. Those in the blinitumomab had better overall survival (71.3% vs 58.4%, p = 0.02, NNT = 8) and numerically better disease-free survival (54.4% vs 39%, HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.47-1.03) at 2 years.

There have been six studies with 333 patients of colony stimulating factor in children with ALL: they found some benefits in terms of reduced duration of hospitalization and infections, but no evidence regarding survival.

An emerging treatment option for relapsed or refractory ALL is the use of CAR-T cells. A study with 153 patients with the primary outcome of remission showed high and durable response rates with obecabtagene autoleucel anti CD19 therapy.

Another used CAR-T cells to target CD7 in 9 children and 2 adults. Nine patients had deep remission and were able to proceed with ste cell transplants, and 7 of 11 were in remission betweeen 3 and 36 months after treatment.

Surgical care is generally not required in the treatment of ALL, except for the placement of a central venous catheter. Such catheters are used for administering chemotherapy, blood products, and antibiotics, and for drawing blood samples.
Provide psychological support for the patient and the family.
To improve outcomes, immediately treat and prevent metabolic and infectious complications.
Control nausea, vomiting, and pain.

Prophylactic oral antibiotics may be appropriate in patients with expected prolonged, profound granulocytopenia (<100/mm3 for 2 weeks). To detect the presence or acquisition of resistant organisms, serial surveillance cultures may be helpful in such patients. Empiric broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy is an absolute necessity for febrile patients who are profoundly neutropenic.

Although individual clinical trials have not shown a reduction in mortality from prophylactic antibiotics in afebrle neutropenic patients, a Cochrane review does demonstrate this benefit, especially for quinolones.
The use of myeloid growth factors during remission induction therapy appears to decrease the time to hematopoietic reconstitution.
Transfuse red blood cells if hemoglobin is less than 8 g/dL or signs and symptoms of anemia exist, and platelets when the platelet count is less than 10,000/mm3 or any signs of bleeding exist.
Instruct patients in personal hygiene to avoid infection.

A Cochrane review of 10 studies has confirmed there is consistent adrenal insufficiency in childhood ALL following cessation of glucocorticoid therapy, suggesting a need for steroid replacement and more investigation into the effect of treatment on the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.
Elaborate isolation facilities, including filtered air, sterile food, and gut flora sterilization are not routinely indicated, but may benefit transplant patients.

In patients being treated with autologous transplant, a double blind RCT of 560 patients (not exclusively leukemic diagnosis) has demonstrated efficacy for inactivated varicella zoster vaccine to reduce infection.
Frequent hospitalizations may be required to administer treatment and to deal with complications of therapy, including the need for blood transfusions or antibiotics.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a complication of acute and chronic leukemia. Human activated protein C, recombinant human soluble thrombomodulin, tranexamic acid and dermatan sulphate have been proposed as therapies, but well designed clinical trials are lacking.

Venous thromboembolism is common in patients receiving an l-asparaginase containing chemotherapy regiment. An observational suggests that this risk is heightened by administration of fibrinogen and heparin, and is not reduced by administration of antithrombin.
Prognosis is predicted by clinical characteristics, immunophenotype, cytogenetic and molecular analysis, and treatment response. C
Favorable prognosis is predicted by age less than 30 years, WBC less than 30,000 at diagnosis, and no chromosomal abnormalities such as Ph chromosome and translocation t(4;11). B
Achieving a CR at the end of the first cycle and a rapid blast clearance are important predictors of outcome. C
Detection of MRD through immunophenotype and PCR analysis is important as a prognostic factor and for the follow-up. C
Survivors of childhood ALL are at long-term increased risk of cancer (up to four-fold increased risk). B

Age appears to be the most important prognostic factor influencing ALL outcomes, with overall survival rates steadily declining with increasing age. Survival has been uniformly poor in the elderly population until the recent incorporation of targeted therapy into chemotherapy strategies for certain subtypes of ALL (eg, Burkitt's ALL or Ph-positive ALL).

A larger leukemia cell burden correlates with a greater likelihood of resistant subclones, irrespective of age. Leukocytosis (WBC >30,000-50,000 cells/mm3 in precursor B-cell ALL or >100,000 cells/mm3 in T-cell ALL) is associated with a higher risk of relapse as well as an increased potential for complications during induction.
CNS disease at presentation influences prognosis if appropriate therapy directed at these sanctuary site is not provided.

Karyotype remains a prognostic indicator of ALL outcomes regardless of the regimen used since the associated molecular aberrations contribute to ALL pathogenesis and thus prognosis. Hyperdiploidy (>50 chromosomes per leukemia cell) is often observed in childhood ALL and confers a favorable prognosis, whereas hypodiploidy (<45 chromosomes per leukemia cell) is unfavorable. The Ph-positive karyotype [t(9;22)(q34;q11)] resulting in a Bcr-Abl fusion protein carried the worst prognosis before the introduction of TKIs directed against Bcr-Abl.The t(4;11)(q21;q23) karyotype associated with the mixed-lineage leukemia (MLL)-AF4 fusion gene portends a particularly dismal prognosis; for these patients, allogeneic SCT during the first CR is indicated.

Outcomes for patients with pro-B-cell ALL are particularly poor, and this appears to be because of the high frequency of t(4;11) karyotypes in this subgroup. Thymic T-cell ALL leukemias have a favorable outcome.
The overexpression of CD20 in non-Burkitt's ALL has been described as a poor prognostic feature in adults, now improved with the introduction of anti-CD20 antibody.

A late CR, which occurs after 3 to 4 weeks from the start of treatment or response after more than 1 course of chemotherapy predicts a higher risk of disease recurrence. Among patients who achieved CRs within 4 weeks, those who had persistent blasts at day 15 fared significantly worse. In an Italian collaborative group study, lack of corticosteroid response following a 7-day course of prednisone immediately before induction negatively affected overall survival. The persistence of circulating blasts at day 7 or the persistence of marrow leukemia at day 14 during induction treatment with hyper-CVAD have predicted for worse outcome.
Hypermethylator phenotypes have a worse outcome.
Outcome also depends on dose of chemotherapy drugs and individual metabolism (6-mercaptopurine), unplanned interval delays between treatments, and withholding of treatment.
A number of prognostic indices have been proposed to better define risk groups at diagnosis and stratify treatment.
A study of 419 children being trated with induction therapy found that a blast count >0.1 x 109/L on Day 8 and platelet count <100 x 109/L on Day 33 were associated with worse survival.

MRD can be identified by the presence of leukemic cells in the bone marrow undetectable through conventional microscopy. This can be accomplished by using either flow cytometry or real-time quantitative PCR to detect fusion transcripts resulting from chromosome abnormalities or patient-specific junctional regions of rearranged immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor genes.
Based on the MRD at different time points, risk groups have been identified. T-ALL shows a slower MRD response.
Risk-adapted therapeutic approaches are being pursued based on these concepts even if appropriate time points, threshold of residual disease, and response criteria still need to be defined.

Survivors of childhood ALL are at long-term increased risk of cancer. In a large cohort with median 19 year follow-up, the cumulative incidence of secondary cancer was 4% at 15 years and 6.3% at 30 years (RR 13.5). Another large cohort study in Ireland found a four-fold increased risk of cancer in childhood survivors of cancer.

The outcome for adults older than 60 years with ALL is worse because of the age-related differences in the pathophysiology of ALL, a higher incidence of poor-risk features in adults compared with children, and a decrease in the ability of elderly patients to tolerate chemotherapy.

These patients have the highest rate of Ph-positive ALL; they usually have more comorbid conditions and are more susceptible to adverse effects and to infections, also because of lower marrow reserves.
